title: A robot moves only right or down on an m by n grid where some cells are blocked (marked 1). Count distinct paths from top-left to bottom-right; blocked cells cannot be entered.
shortTitle: Unique Paths II — grid paths with obstacles

s1_definition.profdef: Grid DP like Unique Paths but any obstacle cell has dp=0, and the first row/column stop contributing once an obstacle is hit. For free cells dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j] + dp[i][j−1]; obstacle cells force dp[i][j]=0. If the start or end is blocked the answer is 0. Time O(m·n), space O(n).
s1_definition.analogy: A courier at National Bank of India routes a document across a grid of offices moving only east or south, but some offices are closed for the day. A closed office contributes zero routes, and any route passing through it is eliminated.
s1_definition.oneliner: Obstacle ⇒ dp=0; free ⇒ from above + from left; blocked start/end ⇒ 0.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Grid DP like Unique Paths but any obstacle cell has dp=0, and the first row/column stop contributing once an obstacle is hit. For free cells dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j] + dp[i][j−1]; obstacle cells force dp[i][j]=0. If the start or end is blocked the answer is 0. Time O(m·n), space O(n).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A courier at National Bank of India routes a document across a grid of offices moving only east or south, but some offices are closed for the day. A closed office contributes zero routes, and any route passing through it is eliminated.

**One line to remember:** Obstacle ⇒ dp=0; free ⇒ from above + from left; blocked start/end ⇒ 0.

sections.s2_technical:
Start by checking the top-left cell: if it is an obstacle the answer is zero because the robot cannot even begin. Otherwise set dp[0][0]=1. Build the dp grid where each obstacle cell is forced to zero and each free cell sums the paths from above and from the left, exactly like the obstacle-free version except for the zeroing. For example: `dp[i][j] = (grid[i][j]==1) ? 0 : (up + left);`.

The first row and first column need care: along an edge, once an obstacle appears, every cell after it is unreachable because there is only one direction of travel, so those cells become zero and stay zero. The summation naturally handles this when you start edges from zero and only add the single valid neighbor.

The time and space are O(m·n), reducible to O(n) with a rolling row that zeroes out obstacle columns. A senior nuance is the easy-to-miss edge case where the destination itself is an obstacle, which must yield zero, and this falls out automatically because that cell is forced to zero.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a courier routes a document across a grid of offices moving only east or south, but some offices are closed and cannot be entered. This is exactly how Unique Paths II works.

Problem 2 — A closed office must eliminate every route through it, including whole edges beyond it. This is exactly why obstacle cells are forced to zero and propagate.

The mini-project builds an `ObstacleRoutePlanner`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a three-by-three grid with a single obstacle in the center.

Step 1: The start cell is free, so dp of zero and zero is one.

Step 2: The first row and first column fill with ones because there are no obstacles along the edges.

Step 3: The center cell is an obstacle, so its dp value is forced to zero, eliminating all routes through it.

Step 4: Interior cells sum their top and left neighbors, but the zeroed center reduces the counts flowing through.

Step 5: The bottom-right cell holds two, and the two-by-two grid with a top-right block yields one.

```text
  obstacle ⇒ dp=0 ; free ⇒ dp[i-1][j]+dp[i][j-1]
  blocked start/end ⇒ 0
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Unique Paths II is the obstacle version of the grid counting problem. I define dp of i and j as the number of distinct paths from the top-left to that cell, moving only right or down. The one addition compared to the obstacle-free version is that any blocked cell is forced to a count of zero, which eliminates every path that would pass through it.

I start by checking the corners: if either the start or the destination is blocked, the answer is zero because the robot cannot begin or finish. For every free cell I sum the paths from directly above and directly to the left, and for every obstacle cell I set the count to zero. The first row and first column need care because once an obstacle appears along an edge, every cell beyond it is unreachable and stays zero, which falls out naturally when I start the edges from zero and add only valid neighbors.

In my project at National Bank of India, a courier routed a document across a grid of offices moving only east or south, but some offices were closed and could not be entered. A closed office had to eliminate every route through it, including whole edges beyond it, so I forced obstacle cells to zero and let the counts propagate, and I can reduce the memory to a single rolling row.
